title: Respiration in Plants
tagline: How plants release energy from food: glycolysis, the Krebs cycle, and what changes when oxygen runs short.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ICSE Class IX Biology syllabus (official-verified baseline, examination year 2027). Every stage, equation and yield below follows standard plant respiration. ATP totals are quoted on the classical textbook basis of 38 per glucose for aerobic respiration. No board examination paper was consulted, so every question is original practice and not a previous year question.

overview.intro: Respiration is the controlled oxidation of food inside a living cell to release energy, and it happens in every living cell of a plant — not only in the parts that appear to be doing something. This chapter begins by setting respiration against photosynthesis, since the two are often confused, then follows a glucose molecule through glycolysis in the cytoplasm and the Krebs cycle in the mitochondrial matrix, naming what enters and what leaves each stage. It then contrasts aerobic respiration, which uses oxygen and extracts nearly all the available energy, with anaerobic respiration, which does not and yields only a fraction of it, and finally covers the standard school experiments that demonstrate gas exchange and heat release during respiration.

learningOutcomes: Write the overall equation for respiration and distinguish respiration from photosynthesis.
Outline glycolysis and the Krebs cycle, giving the site, the raw materials and the products of each.
Compare aerobic and anaerobic respiration in terms of oxygen, products, energy yield and where each occurs.
Describe the experiments that demonstrate carbon dioxide release, oxygen use and heat evolution during respiration.

learn.title: What respiration is and how it differs from photosynthesis

blocks.text: Respiration is a catabolic process in which food, chiefly glucose, is oxidised step by step inside the living cell and the energy stored in its bonds is released and trapped in molecules of ATP. The overall equation can be written as glucose plus oxygen giving carbon dioxide, water and energy, and it is the exact reverse of the photosynthesis equation in its chemicals, but not in its energy flow. Photosynthesis is an anabolic, endergonic process that builds complex molecules and stores energy; respiration is a catabolic, exergonic process that breaks molecules down and releases energy. The two are not opposites in the sense that one stops when the other runs: a green leaf carries out both simultaneously in daylight, photosynthesis only at night, and respiration continuously, day and night, in every living cell including the roots, which never see light at all. Respiration proceeds through a series of enzyme-controlled steps rather than a single burn, which is why energy is released in manageable packets instead of being lost at once as heat.

blocks.caption: Respiration compared with photosynthesis
rows: Carbon dioxide, water, energy as ATP
All day and night, in every living cell
Only in daylight and only in green cells

items: Respiration is continuous; photosynthesis is intermittent and depends on light, so respiration always runs.
The energy released by respiration is trapped as ATP, the cell's immediate energy currency.
Because respiration proceeds in steps through enzymes, much of the energy is captured rather than lost as heat.
Roots, seeds and other non-green cells respire but cannot photosynthesise at all.
A plant kept in the dark loses weight as stored food is respired away, since nothing is being made to replace it.
Respiration is a controlled oxidation — enzymes control each step, unlike the uncontrolled burning of glucose in a flame.
The respiratory equation is balanced: one glucose, six oxygens, six carbons out as carbon dioxide, six waters.
All living cells respire, but only green cells in light photosynthesise.

items.text: A green leaf in bright sunlight absorbs more carbon dioxide in photosynthesis than it releases in respiration, so the net gas exchange is uptake; at night, with photosynthesis stopped, it takes in oxygen and gives out carbon dioxide only.
items.note: This is why a sealed jar with a plant turns oxygen-poor over a day and night.

items.text: A seed germinating in a dark cupboard gains no energy from light at all: every joule it uses comes from respiring the food stored in its cotyledons or endosperm.
items.note: Germination is the clearest demonstration that respiration does not require light.

learn.title: Glycolysis: the first stage in the cytoplasm

blocks.text: Glycolysis is the splitting of a glucose molecule, a six-carbon compound, into two molecules of pyruvate, a three-carbon compound, and it takes place in the cytoplasm, outside the mitochondria. The pathway has a preparatory phase that costs two ATP molecules to phosphorylate and rearrange the glucose, followed by a payoff phase that generates four ATP and reduces two NAD molecules to NADH. The net result is therefore two ATP, two molecules of NADH and two pyruvate from each glucose. Glycolysis requires no oxygen, which is why it is the one stage common to both aerobic and anaerobic respiration, and it can proceed in the absence of mitochondria — in prokaryotes, in the cytoplasm of every cell, and in plant cells at all times. The pyruvate it produces then has two possible fates: if oxygen is available it enters the mitochondrion and is fully oxidised; if it is not, it is fermented instead.

items.meaning: The splitting of glucose into two molecules of pyruvate in the cytoplasm; literally sugar splitting.
The three-carbon product of glycolysis that feeds into either the Krebs cycle or fermentation.
Adenosine triphosphate, the molecule in which a cell stores usable energy in high-energy phosphate bonds.
A coenzyme that accepts electrons and hydrogen; reduced NAD carries them to the next stage of respiration.
Making ATP directly by transferring a phosphate from a substrate, as happens twice in glycolysis.
Requiring oxygen; used of respiration that fully oxidises food.

blocks.caption: Accounting for one glucose molecule in glycolysis

items: Glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm and is independent of oxygen, so it is common to aerobic and anaerobic respiration.
One 6-carbon glucose becomes two 3-carbon pyruvate molecules — the split is the meaning of the word glycolysis.
Two ATP are invested early and four are produced later, so the net gain is two ATP.
The stage also reduces two NAD molecules, and those carry hydrogen to the mitochondrion in aerobic conditions.
Glycolysis alone releases only a small fraction of the energy stored in glucose.
Because it needs no organelle, glycolysis can run in any living cell, including bacteria that have no mitochondria.
The preparatory investment of ATP is why the net yield is not four.
Pyruvate's fate depends entirely on whether oxygen is present when glycolysis finishes.

items.text: In a yeast cell kept without oxygen the pyruvate from glycolysis is decarboxylated to acetaldehyde and then reduced to ethanol, releasing carbon dioxide; the cell gains only the two ATP from glycolysis.
items.note: This is the alcohol fermentation used in brewing and baking.

items.text: In an animal muscle working faster than blood can deliver oxygen, pyruvate is reduced to lactic acid instead, and the ache felt afterwards comes partly from that accumulation.
items.note: Plants ferment too, but the standard plant product is ethanol and carbon dioxide.

learn.title: The Krebs cycle and the complete oxidation of pyruvate

blocks.text: When oxygen is available, each pyruvate moves into the mitochondrial matrix and is first decarboxylated and combined with coenzyme A to give acetyl coenzyme A, releasing one molecule of carbon dioxide. The acetyl group then enters the Krebs cycle, a cyclic series of reactions in which the two-carbon acetyl combines with a four-carbon oxaloacetate to form a six-carbon citrate. Through a sequence of rearrangements, decarboxylations and dehydrogenations, two carbons leave as carbon dioxide and the four-carbon oxaloacetate is regenerated so the cycle can turn again. Each turn reduces three NAD molecules and one FAD, and produces one ATP directly by substrate-level phosphorylation. Because each glucose gives two pyruvate, the cycle turns twice per glucose, producing two ATP, six NADH, two FADH2 and four carbon dioxide molecules. The reduced coenzymes then carry their hydrogen to the inner mitochondrial membrane.

blocks.caption: Per glucose molecule, aerobic respiration from pyruvate onwards
rows: Water formed as oxygen accepts hydrogen

items: The Krebs cycle is a cycle because the four-carbon acceptor is regenerated at the end of each turn.
Carbon dioxide is released at two points — the link reaction and the decarboxylation steps within the cycle.
Most of the energy released from glucose is not in ATP yet; it is held in reduced NAD and FAD awaiting the electron transport chain.
The cycle needs oxygen indirectly: without it the coenzymes cannot be reoxidised and the cycle stalls.
Acetyl CoA is the common entry point for the breakdown of carbohydrates, fats and proteins, all three of which can feed the cycle.
The inner mitochondrial membrane carries the electron transport chain, whose folding into cristae increases the surface available.
Oxaloacetate is regenerated each turn, which is what makes the sequence a cycle rather than a linear pathway.
Water is formed at the end of the electron transport chain when oxygen accepts electrons, hydrogen ions and electrons.

items.text: Tracking one glucose: two pyruvate give two acetyl CoA and two carbon dioxide in the link reaction, then two turns of the cycle give four more carbon dioxide — six carbons out for the six that entered.
items.note: Counting carbons proves the six carbon dioxide in the balanced equation.

items.text: Starving a plant of oxygen blocks the electron transport chain, reduced coenzymes accumulate, and the whole cycle grinds to a halt even though glucose and enzymes are still present.
items.note: Oxygen is needed at the end, which is why its absence stops the beginning as well.

learn.title: Aerobic against anaerobic respiration, and the experiments

blocks.text: Aerobic respiration uses oxygen to oxidise food completely to carbon dioxide and water, and because every stage runs, it extracts a large proportion of the energy stored in glucose — classically 38 ATP per molecule, with modern estimates nearer 36. It occurs in the cytoplasm and mitochondria and its products are harmless to the cell. Anaerobic respiration occurs without oxygen and stops at an incompletely oxidised product: in plants and yeast, glucose breaks down to ethanol and carbon dioxide; in animal muscle it breaks down to lactic acid. Because only glycolysis operates, the yield is just the two ATP from that stage, so far less energy is released and most remains locked in the organic product. The two experiments most often asked about rest on the same detectable changes: carbon dioxide can be shown by passing the air from germinating seeds into lime water, which turns milky; oxygen use can be shown by a respirometer or by the rise in water level in a sealed flask; and heat release can be shown by placing germinating seeds in an insulated flask with dry seeds as the control, where only the germinating seeds raise the thermometer.

blocks.caption: Aerobic against anaerobic respiration
rows: Glycolysis, link reaction, Krebs cycle, electron transport chain
Ethanol and carbon dioxide in plants and yeast; lactic acid in animals
38 ATP per glucose on the classical accounting
Most of the available energy released
Most of the energy remains in the ethanol or lactic acid
Yeast in a sealed vessel; a sprinting muscle

items: Lime water turns milky with carbon dioxide, which is the standard test used in the germinating-seed experiment.
A controlled experiment must include dry seeds as a control so that the change is attributed to germination rather than to the apparatus.
A respirometer measures oxygen uptake by the fall in gas volume, with a small tube of alkali absorbing the carbon dioxide given out.
Heat from germinating seeds is detected by a thermometer in an insulated flask of soaked seeds against one of dry seeds.
Anaerobic respiration is not the absence of respiration; it is an oxygen-independent pathway with a lower yield.
Ethanol fermentation is used in brewing and in baking, where the carbon dioxide makes bread rise.
Lactic acid accumulation in muscle causes fatigue, and oxygen repaid afterwards is called the oxygen debt.
Anaerobic pathways are valuable precisely because they are fast when oxygen cannot be delivered quickly enough.

items.text: Sealed under water, germinating seeds release bubbles that turn lime water milky while a control of dry seeds produces none, demonstrating that carbon dioxide is a product of germination.
items.note: The control is what converts an observation into evidence.

items.text: In bread dough, yeast ferments the flour sugars to ethanol and carbon dioxide; the gas expands in the oven and sets the crumb while the ethanol evaporates, leaving no taste of alcohol.
items.note: One fermentation, both products accounted for in a familiar food.

items.meaning: Anaerobic breakdown of pyruvate to ethanol and carbon dioxide in plants and yeast, or to lactic acid in animals.
The volume of carbon dioxide given out divided by the volume of oxygen taken in during respiration.
The extra oxygen needed after strenuous exercise to oxidise the lactic acid accumulated in muscle.
A sealed apparatus that measures the rate of gas exchange by a germinating seed or small organism.

figures.description: A cell outline containing a mitochondrion drawn with a double membrane and folded cristae. A glucose molecule is shown in the cytoplasm splitting into two pyruvate with two ATP gained. The pyruvate crosses into the mitochondrial matrix, loses carbon dioxide to become acetyl CoA, and enters a circular arrow representing the Krebs cycle that releases carbon dioxide, reduced coenzymes and ATP. A further arrow runs along the inner membrane for the electron transport chain, ending with water and a large ATP tally.

The branch on the left continues through acetyl CoA and the Krebs cycle to six carbon dioxide and six water, with a stack of ATP totalling 38. The branch on the right ends at ethanol plus carbon dioxide with two ATP, labelled anaerobic in plants and yeast.

A delivery tube leads from the flask into a test tube of clear lime water. keyPoints: Respiration is the step-by-step oxidation of food inside living cells to release energy trapped as ATP.
Respiration is catabolic and releases energy; photosynthesis is anabolic and stores energy, and both can run at once in a green leaf.
Glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm, needs no oxygen, and splits one glucose into two pyruvate with a net gain of 2 ATP.
The link reaction converts pyruvate to acetyl CoA and releases the first carbon dioxide.
The Krebs cycle turns in the mitochondrial matrix, releasing carbon dioxide, reduced coenzymes and one ATP per turn.
The electron transport chain on the inner mitochondrial membrane uses oxygen and yields most of the ATP, forming water.
Aerobic respiration gives carbon dioxide and water and classically 38 ATP per glucose.
Anaerobic respiration in plants and yeast gives ethanol and carbon dioxide with only 2 ATP per glucose.
Anaerobic respiration in animal muscle gives lactic acid, and the extra oxygen needed afterwards is the oxygen debt.
Lime water turns milky in the presence of carbon dioxide, which underpins the germinating-seed experiment.
examFocus: Write the respiration equation balanced and with an arrow that includes energy — an unbalanced equation or one missing energy loses a mark immediately.
Stage questions need site as well as products: glycolysis in the cytoplasm, the Krebs cycle in the mitochondrial matrix, the electron transport chain on the inner membrane.
Yield questions expect 38 ATP for aerobic and 2 for anaerobic, plus the reason anaerobic is so much lower — only glycolysis runs.
Experiment answers must name the control and the specific observation, not just the apparatus, because the comparison is what demonstrates the result.

vocabulary.meaning: Controlled oxidation of food in living cells to release energy as ATP.
Splitting of glucose into two pyruvate molecules in the cytoplasm.
Three-carbon product of glycolysis that enters either the Krebs cycle or fermentation.
Cyclic reactions in the mitochondrial matrix that release carbon dioxide and reduce coenzymes.
Adenosine triphosphate, the cell's immediate energy currency.
Anaerobic breakdown of pyruvate to ethanol and carbon dioxide, or to lactic acid.
Volume of carbon dioxide released divided by volume of oxygen taken up.
Oxygen required after exercise to repay the lactic acid formed anaerobically.

questions.prompt: In which part of the cell does glycolysis take place?
questions.explanation: Glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm, outside any organelle, which is why it can run in cells that lack mitochondria entirely, such as bacteria, and why it is the one stage shared by both aerobic and anaerobic respiration. The Krebs cycle is in the mitochondrial matrix, the electron transport chain on the inner mitochondrial membrane, and the stroma of the chloroplast is the site of photosynthesis.
questions.commonMistake: Placing glycolysis in the mitochondrion because the rest of respiration happens there. It is specifically the cytoplasmic stage.

questions.prompt: Glycolysis splits one six-carbon glucose molecule into two three-carbon molecules of __________, with a net gain of __________ molecules of ATP.
questions.explanation: Glycolysis literally means sugar splitting: the six-carbon glucose is broken into two three-carbon pyruvate molecules. Two ATP molecules are invested in the preparatory phase and four are produced in the payoff phase, so the net gain is two ATP per glucose.
questions.commonMistake: Quoting four ATP as the yield. Four are made but two are spent first, so the net gain is two.

questions.prompt: Which set of products is correctly matched to anaerobic respiration in a plant cell?
questions.explanation: Without oxygen, only glycolysis and fermentation operate in a plant or yeast cell: pyruvate is converted to ethanol and carbon dioxide and just the two ATP from glycolysis are gained. Carbon dioxide and water with 38 ATP describe aerobic respiration, lactic acid is the anaerobic product in animal muscle, and acetyl coenzyme A is an aerobic intermediate.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing lactic acid for a plant. Lactic acid fermentation is the animal muscle pathway; plants and yeast make ethanol.

questions.prompt: State two ways in which respiration differs from photosynthesis.
questions.answer: Respiration is a catabolic process that breaks down glucose and releases energy, whereas photosynthesis is an anabolic process that builds glucose and stores energy taken from light. Second, respiration occurs in every living cell of the plant at all times, day and night, while photosynthesis occurs only in green cells and only when light is present.
questions.explanation: Two differences are required, and the pair that carries most credit is the energy change and the conditions of occurrence. Stating the raw materials and products works equally well as the first point, since they are the mirror image of each other, but each difference must be given as a contrast rather than as a fact about one process alone.
questions.commonMistake: Describing only respiration. A difference is a comparison, so both sides of each point must appear.

questions.prompt: Outline what happens during the Krebs cycle, stating where it occurs, what enters it, and what is produced per turn.
questions.answer: The Krebs cycle takes place in the matrix of the mitochondrion. It begins when the two-carbon acetyl group of acetyl coenzyme A, formed from pyruvate, combines with the four-carbon compound oxaloacetate to form a six-carbon citrate. As citrate passes through the series of reactions of the cycle it is rearranged, decarboxylated and dehydrogenated: two carbons leave as carbon dioxide, three NAD molecules are reduced to NADH, one FAD is reduced to FADH2, and one ATP is produced directly by substrate-level phosphorylation. The four-carbon oxaloacetate is regenerated, ready to accept the next acetyl group, which is what makes the pathway a cycle. Because each glucose gives two pyruvate, the cycle turns twice for every glucose molecule oxidised.
questions.explanation: The answer must state the site, the incoming acceptor and the products per turn, and it must explain why the pathway is called a cycle — the regeneration of oxaloacetate. Mentioning that it turns twice per glucose connects the cycle back to the overall equation.
questions.commonMistake: Naming carbon dioxide as a product but not saying where the carbons come from. They come from the acetyl group passing through the cycle, which is the point of the decarboxylation steps.

questions.prompt: Why does anaerobic respiration release far less energy from each glucose than aerobic respiration?
options: Because glucose is broken down more slowly without oxygen
Because only glycolysis and fermentation operate, so the Krebs cycle and electron transport chain never run
Because the ATP produced is immediately used up by the cell
Because oxygen is needed to make glucose in the first place
questions.answer: Because only glycolysis and fermentation operate, so the Krebs cycle and electron transport chain never run
questions.explanation: Almost all of the energy stored in glucose is released in the Krebs cycle and, above all, in the electron transport chain. Without oxygen those coenzymes cannot be reoxidised and both stages stop, so only the two ATP of glycolysis are obtained and the rest of the energy remains locked in the ethanol or lactic acid that is formed.
questions.commonMistake: Saying anaerobic respiration releases energy more slowly. Slowness would not change the total yield; the missing stages do.

questions.prompt: Describe an experiment to demonstrate that germinating seeds release carbon dioxide during respiration. Give the apparatus, the observation, the control you would set up, and what the control proves.
questions.answer: Place a quantity of soaked, germinating seeds in a beaker inside a conical flask and seal the flask with a stopper carrying a thistle funnel that reaches down to the beaker and a delivery tube leading out of the flask. Pass the delivery tube into a test tube of clear lime water. Allow the apparatus to stand for several hours, then blow air gently through the thistle funnel to sweep the gases from the flask into the lime water. The lime water turns milky or cloudy, which is the positive test for carbon dioxide, showing that the seeds have released it. The control uses the same apparatus with the same volume of dry, non-germinating seeds in place of the germinating ones, and the lime water remains clear, proving that the carbon dioxide came from the living process of germination rather than from the apparatus, the seeds themselves as inert material or the air in the flask.
questions.explanation: Four elements are required: apparatus, positive observation, control, and the conclusion the control supports. The control is the part most often omitted, yet it is what allows the carbon dioxide to be attributed to respiration rather than to the flask or to air already present, so it carries its own marks.
questions.commonMistake: Setting up the experiment with no control. Without dry seeds as a comparison, the milky lime water proves only that carbon dioxide was present.

questions.prompt: Explain how you would show that heat is given out during germination, and state why a control is included.
questions.answer: Take two vacuum flasks, one containing soaked germinating seeds and one containing the same number and mass of dry seeds, and insert a thermometer into each, sealing the flasks. Leave them for several hours and read both thermometers at intervals. The flask containing the germinating seeds shows a higher temperature than the flask of dry seeds, showing that heat is evolved during germination. The dry seeds act as a control because they are identical in every respect except that they are not germinating, so any temperature rise above theirs can be attributed to the metabolic activity of germination rather than to the room temperature, the flask or the thermometer.
questions.explanation: The apparatus must be described with both flasks, the observation is a temperature difference rather than an absolute value, and the control's role must be stated as excluding alternative explanations. Comparing readings between the two flasks, not merely watching one rise, is what demonstrates the release of heat.
questions.commonMistake: Reporting a single thermometer rising. Without the dry-seed comparison the rise could simply be the room warming.

questions.prompt: Which of the following gases turns lime water milky and is therefore used to test for a product of respiration?
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide reacts with limewater, which is calcium hydroxide solution, to form insoluble calcium carbonate, and the suspension appears milky or cloudy. This is the standard identification used in the germinating-seed experiment. Oxygen does not react with limewater, nitrogen does not, and water vapour simply condenses.
questions.commonMistake: Confusing the gas with the test for oxygen, which uses a glowing splint that relights rather than a chemical solution.

questions.prompt: During aerobic respiration the __________ cycle takes place in the matrix of the mitochondrion, while the electron transport chain lies on the folded __________ of the same organelle.
questions.explanation: The Krebs cycle reactions occur free in the fluid matrix of the mitochondrion, where the enzymes and coenzymes are dissolved. The electron transport chain is built into the inner mitochondrial membrane, and its folding into cristae greatly increases the surface area available for the chain and for the ATP synthase that uses the proton gradient to make ATP.
questions.commonMistake: Writing 'cristae' for the second blank as if it were a separate structure. Cristae are the folds of the inner membrane, not a distinct layer.

questions.prompt: A water plant is kept in the dark for 24 hours and then placed in a test tube of water with a funnel over it. Bubbles rising from the cut stem are collected and found to relight a glowing splint. Explain what is happening, and state why the plant was kept in the dark before the test.
questions.answer: The bubbles are oxygen, since oxygen relights a glowing splint. The plant is releasing it as a product of respiration: every living cell is oxidising stored food, and the oxygen given out is what is being collected. The plant was kept in the dark beforehand so that photosynthesis was stopped — in light a green plant would take in carbon dioxide and release oxygen from photosynthesis, which would be indistinguishable from the oxygen of respiration. Keeping it dark allows the stored food reserve to build up and ensures that the only gas exchange occurring during the collection is that of respiration.
questions.explanation: The identity of the gas rests on the splint test, and the reason for the dark period is the heart of the question: light would start photosynthesis, which also produces oxygen, so the source of the gas could not be attributed to respiration alone. Stating only that the plant needs darkness misses the point about distinguishing the two processes.
questions.commonMistake: Saying the plant was darkened to make it respire. Plants respire continuously; the darkening removes the competing oxygen source of photosynthesis.
